title: CP-Agent: A Harness-Engineered Agent for Crystal Plasticity Simulation Workflows
authors: Samuel Onimpa Alfred, Abhishek Kumar, Veera Sundararaghavan
abstract: Crystal plasticity (CP) simulations predict the mechanical behavior of polycrystalline metals, yet their routine use is hindered by the manual effort of configuring heterogeneous tools, orchestrating multi-step data pipelines, and calibrating constitutive parameters against experiments. These bottlenecks impede productivity in systematic parameter studies, motivating interest in automated workflows. This study presents CP-Agent, a harness-engineered LLM-based agent that autonomously executes complete CP modeling workflows from natural-language tasks. Operating under the ReAct paradigm, the agent reasons about tool selection and sequencing while delegating numerical search to established optimizers. The harness comprises a minimal system prompt, typed tool definitions, a dispatcher, and a safety-bounded iteration loop, encoding domain knowledge through tool schemas rather than hard-coded logic. CP-Agent is demonstrated on four case studies: calibrating four slip parameters of additively manufactured stainless steel 316L against tensile data; validating the workflow against published copper benchmarks, reproducing stress-strain and texture evolution; recovering the initial crystallographic texture of copper, where the agent correctly identifies a diffuse initial texture; and reproducing the multi-pass rolling texture evolution of a Mg-Zn-Ca alloy, where the agent chains five deformation passes and recovers the experimentally observed weakened, split basal texture. In all cases, the agent inferred the correct execution sequence from the task statement, robustly across repeated runs, and delivered physically interpretable results. This work establishes harness engineering as a systematic approach to automating CP modeling workflows while maintaining physical interpretability and auditability through visible reasoning traces.

infographic.key_insight: CP-Agent uses a harness-engineered LLM agent to autonomously plan and execute complete crystal plasticity workflows from natural-language instructions while keeping decisions interpretable through visible reasoning traces.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It can reduce the manual burden of calibration, benchmarking, and multi-step simulation setup for polycrystalline metal constitutive modeling, enabling faster and more systematic parameter studies.
method: ReAct-style agent for reasoning over tool choice and execution order
Typed tool schemas, dispatcher, and safety-bounded iteration loop form the harness
Numerical search is delegated to established optimizers rather than the LLM
infographic.evidence_signal: The agent was evaluated on four case studies, including stainless steel 316L calibration, copper benchmark validation and texture recovery, and Mg-Zn-Ca multi-pass rolling texture evolution, with correct workflow sequencing and physically interpretable results across repeated runs.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on well-designed tool interfaces and bounded execution, so robustness may drop if the workflow tools, schemas, or domain assumptions are incomplete or poorly specified.
infographic.paper_title: CP-Agent: A Harness-Engineered Agent for Crystal Plasticity Simulation Workflows

title: Tessellated Isotropic Elastic Lattice Spring Model for Quasi-Brittle Fracture
authors: D. M. LI, Meng-Cheng HE
abstract: Quasi-brittle fracture is prevalent in concrete, rock, ceramics, composites, and masonry, and its simulation faces a trade-off among accuracy, efficiency, and simplicity. The classical Lattice Spring Model (LSM) captures cracking via bond breakage without remeshing, but its elements are empirical and limited to a few tessellable shapes with fixed Poisson's ratios. We propose a tessellated Isotropic Elastic Lattice Spring Model (IELSM) that discretizes continua into polygonal elements with axial springs and a volumetric constraint, achieving isotropic elasticity on arbitrary polygonal tessellations. Macroscopic isotropy reduces to governing equations whose solvability gives a theoretical criterion for element admissibility, proving conventional tessellable elements and extending to arbitrary regular N-gons and concave elements. Exploiting boundary interpolation compatibility with finite elements, IELSM is assembled by direct node sharing, without interface elements or kinematic constraints. Coupled with an isotropic damage model, a pure bending test and four fracture benchmarks show that the coupling preserves displacement accuracy, yields crack paths and load-displacement curves agreeing with experiments and outperforming standard FEM, and is insensitive to mesh refinement. IELSM can also be restricted to damage-prone regions, with the remainder modeled by finite elements via node sharing. For the benchmarks, this reduces nodes by 41.2-80.9% and CPU time by 34.2-85.2% versus full-domain IELSM. The framework advances IELSM element construction from empirical trial and error to theoretical determination and simplifies coupling to node sharing, offering a balanced route for complex quasi-brittle fracture analysis.

infographic.key_insight: IELSM replaces empirical lattice elements with a theoretically admissible polygonal spring formulation that delivers isotropic elasticity and fracture simulation on arbitrary tessellations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It enables efficient quasi-brittle fracture modeling for concrete, rock, ceramics, composites, and masonry while simplifying FEM coupling through direct node sharing.
method: Discretize continua into polygonal cells with axial springs plus a volumetric constraint to enforce isotropic elasticity.
Derive admissible element shapes from governing equations, extending beyond classical tessellable LSM geometries.
Couple IELSM with an isotropic damage model and optionally restrict it to damage-prone regions while the rest is modeled by FEM.
infographic.evidence_signal: Benchmarks including a pure bending test and four fracture cases showed good agreement with experiments, preserved displacement accuracy, and improved efficiency, including 41.2-80.9% fewer nodes and 34.2-85.2% lower CPU time versus full-domain IELSM in coupled runs.
infographic.watch_item: Element admissibility and damage calibration depend on the theoretical constraints and constitutive model, so implementation must ensure the chosen polygonal mesh satisfies the IELSM criteria.
infographic.paper_title: Tessellated Isotropic Elastic Lattice Spring Model for Quasi-Brittle Fracture

title: Growth-Inspired Graph Generation and Inverse Design of Mechanical Lattices via Dot Matrices Database Augmentation and GCNN
authors: Weiyun Xu, Jiamu Liu
abstract: Natural load-bearing and transport networks are not assembled in a single step; they emerge through a temporally ordered process of growth, branching, reinforcement, and loop formation. Inspired by this developmental logic, this work introduces a morphogenetic graph-generation framework for mechanical lattices in which a discrete dot matrix provides potential nodes and the final architecture is created by sequential cross-layer and intra-layer growth. The same rule is visualized in two dimensions as a leaf-vein-like developmental sequence and implemented in three dimensions on a 3x3x3 nodal matrix containing 27 candidate nodes. A dataset of distinct three-dimensional lattices was evaluated by beam-based finite element analysis and represented directly as graphs. A graph convolutional neural network (GCNN) with three graph-convolution layers and dual global pooling learns the topology-property mapping and predicts effective compressive stiffness. Coupling the GCNN surrogate with rapid structural sampling enables inverse design: for a target stiffness of 1000 MPa, the selected design was predicted at 1042.43 MPa and validated by finite element analysis at 1027.49 MPa. Beyond straight members, the framework has also been extended to parameterized horseshoe-shaped curved beams made of nonlinear materials, enabling topology-geometry design toward prescribed deformation shapes. Our work provides a paradigm for augmenting the database of mechanical metamaterials, and the resulting perspective links biological morphogenesis, graph learning, and nonlinear shape programming in a unified generative design framework for architected materials.

infographic.key_insight: A morphogenetic graph-growth rule, inspired by biological development, can generate mechanical lattices and enable inverse design through a GCNN surrogate.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework offers a practical way to expand mechanical metamaterial databases and rapidly target stiffness or deformation performance without exhaustive finite-element search.
method: Start from a 3×3×3 dot-matrix of 27 candidate nodes and grow the lattice sequentially via cross-layer and intra-layer connections.
Represent each lattice as a graph and train a 3-layer GCNN with dual global pooling to learn topology-to-stiffness mapping.
Use the GCNN as a fast surrogate for sampling and inverse design; extend the idea to curved horseshoe-shaped beams for shape programming.
infographic.evidence_signal: The inverse-design example targeted 1000 MPa and produced a design predicted at 1042.43 MPa, which finite-element analysis validated at 1027.49 MPa.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on the diversity and coverage of the generated lattice database, so extrapolation to unseen topologies or material behaviors may be limited.
infographic.paper_title: Growth-Inspired Graph Generation and Inverse Design of Mechanical Lattices via Dot Matrices Database Augmentation and GCNN

title: Mixed-Dimensional Electromechanical Coupling of Embedded Beam Networks in Soft Dielectric Composites
authors: L. River Spencer, Manuel K. Rausch, Chad Landis, Jan N. Fuhg
abstract: Soft electroactive composites can exhibit strongly architecture-dependent mechanical and electrical responses, but explicitly resolving dense fiber networks in three dimensions is computationally expensive. We develop a mixed-dimensional finite-element formulation in which electroactive fibers are represented by geometrically exact beams embedded in a deformable dielectric matrix. Unlike existing electroactive beam formulations in which the electric potential is defined directly on the beam, the embedded fibers here are driven by the three-dimensional electric field of the surrounding matrix. The matrix field is sampled along the beam centerlines and enters the beam dielectric enthalpy directly, providing two-way electromechanical coupling without introducing independent electric-potential degrees of freedom on the beams. Beam and matrix mechanics are coupled through projected mortar constraints, and the electromechanical problem is solved monolithically. We use the formulation as the microscale model in a periodic homogenization framework to compute effective stress and electric displacement. Verification studies quantify discretization and field-sampling sensitivity, followed by structured and irregular network examples that demonstrate architecture-dependent mechanical and electrical responses without body-fitted three-dimensional fiber meshes.

infographic.key_insight: A mixed-dimensional finite-element model lets embedded electroactive beam networks respond to the surrounding 3D electric field, enabling two-way electromechanical coupling without giving the beams their own electric-potential unknowns.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a much more efficient way to simulate and homogenize dense fiber-reinforced soft dielectric composites, capturing architecture-dependent mechanical and electrical behavior without full 3D fiber meshes.
method: Geometrically exact electroactive beams are embedded in a deformable dielectric matrix.
The matrix electric field is sampled along beam centerlines and used in the beam dielectric enthalpy.
Beam-matrix mechanics are enforced with projected mortar constraints and solved monolithically.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports verification studies on discretization and field-sampling sensitivity, then applies the model to structured and irregular network examples to show architecture-dependent responses.
infographic.watch_item: Accuracy depends on the sampling and constraint projection between the matrix field and beam centerlines, so coarse discretization or poor embedding could affect results.
infographic.paper_title: Mixed-Dimensional Electromechanical Coupling of Embedded Beam Networks in Soft Dielectric Composites

title: Lattice Structure Optimization for Additive Manufacturing: Manufacturability-Driven Design and Pareto Front Construction
authors: Yu Xing, Yang Liu, Lin Lu
abstract: Lattice metamaterials support lightweight, multifunctional structures, while additive manufacturing (AM) enables complex geometries. Yet multiphysics lattice design faces two challenges: efficiently constructing well-covered multi-objective Pareto fronts under limited budgets, and satisfying manufacturing constraints such as overhangs, enclosed cavities, and restricted powder-removal channels. We propose a manufacturing-constraint-driven method for lattice optimization and Pareto-front construction. Differentiable manufacturing constraints are embedded in inverse-homogenization topology optimization, enabling joint optimization of physical performance and manufacturability. A progressive Pareto-front mechanism uses a density-generation network to learn latent representations of high-quality lattices, interpolates neighboring nondominated representations, and decodes them into initial density fields for subsequent optimization. Newly found nondominated solutions update the network and sample set, progressively expanding the manufacturable set. On 3D periodic unit cells, with 1000 optimization runs, network initialization achieves a 92.60% success rate and 916 manufacturable samples, versus 78.30% and 776 for random initialization. Its Pareto front reaches a hypervolume of 0.0787, compared with 0.0675 for random initialization. The results show that the method efficiently constructs broadly covered manufacturable Pareto fronts for multiple physical properties.

infographic.key_insight: The paper couples differentiable manufacturing constraints with inverse-homogenization optimization and a progressive Pareto-front learning strategy to efficiently generate manufacturable lattice designs.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This helps additive manufacturing engineers design lattice metamaterials that better balance performance and printability, while exploring multiple objectives under limited optimization budgets.
method: Embed differentiable constraints for overhangs, enclosed cavities, and powder-removal channels directly into topology optimization.
Use a density-generation network to learn latent representations of high-quality lattices and initialize new optimizations from interpolated nondominated samples.
Iteratively update the network with newly found nondominated solutions to expand the manufacturable Pareto set.
infographic.evidence_signal: On 3D periodic unit cells across 1000 optimization runs, network initialization improved success rate to 92.60% and produced 916 manufacturable samples versus 78.30% and 776 for random initialization, with hypervolume increasing from 0.0675 to 0.0787.
infographic.watch_item: The approach depends on learned initializations and constraint formulations, so performance may vary with lattice class, material system, and the fidelity of manufacturing constraints used in practice.
infographic.paper_title: Lattice Structure Optimization for Additive Manufacturing: Manufacturability-Driven Design and Pareto Front Construction

title: TopoMamba: A Load-Support Relation-Guided Multi-Directional State-Space Model for Topology Optimization
authors: Bin Lou, Yuxuan Cheng, Huaizhi Zong, Junhui Zhang, Bing Xu
abstract: Deep learning has emerged as an efficient alternative for predicting high-performance material distributions in topology optimization. Existing methods struggle to accurately capture load-transfer information, limiting out-of-distribution generalization, while their model architectures often incur high computational costs. To address these challenges, this paper proposes TopoMamba, a topology prediction framework incorporating a load-support relation-guided multi-directional state-space model. Coupling physical fields with load-support relations enables more effective modeling of mechanical dependencies. A load-support relation-guided spatially adaptive fusion mechanism dynamically adjusts multi-directional scan features according to spatial conditions. Mamba is coupled with the solid isotropic material with penalty method to enhance structural mechanical performance while maintaining computational efficiency. Results on two-dimensional topology optimization benchmarks demonstrate that TopoMamba achieves superior topology prediction accuracy, out-of-distribution generalization, and computational efficiency over state-of-the-art models. The proposed load-support physics-guided framework enables efficient optimization of more complex structural systems.

infographic.key_insight: TopoMamba improves topology prediction by combining load-support physics with a multi-directional Mamba state-space model to better capture mechanical dependencies.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework offers a more efficient and generalizable surrogate for topology optimization, helping design stronger structures with lower compute cost.
method: Guides feature learning using load-support relations between physical fields.
Uses spatially adaptive fusion to weight multi-directional scan features by local conditions.
Couples Mamba with SIMP to improve mechanical performance while keeping computation efficient.
infographic.evidence_signal: On two-dimensional topology optimization benchmarks, the method reports superior prediction accuracy, out-of-distribution generalization, and computational efficiency versus state-of-the-art models.
infographic.watch_item: Performance is demonstrated on 2D benchmarks, so scalability to more complex 3D or highly nonlinear structural settings remains to be validated.
infographic.paper_title: TopoMamba: A Load-Support Relation-Guided Multi-Directional State-Space Model for Topology Optimization

title: Finite Element Approximation of a Hemivariational Inequality for Steady-State Heat Conduction: Double-Limit Convergence of Penalization and Discretization
authors: Piotr Bartman-Szwarc, Anna Ochal, Domingo A. Tarzia
abstract: In this paper we study the numerical approximation and convergence analysis of a steady-state heat conduction problem with mixed boundary conditions. The physical model is governed by a hemivariational inequality depending on a heat transfer parameter $α> 0$. We consider the finite element approximation of this penalized problem, as well as its corresponding limit problem with a prescribed constant temperature on a part of the boundary. The main theoretical result establishes the strong convergence of the discrete solutions. Specifically, we prove the double-limit convergence of the finite element approximations to the limit solution as the mesh size $h$ tends to zero and the penalization parameter $α$ tends to infinity, independently and simultaneously. We further complement the convergence analysis with an error estimate of optimal order for the discrete limit problem, and we explain why an estimate uniform in the penalization parameter cannot be expected. The theoretical results are illustrated by numerical simulations on four examples verified by the method of manufactured solutions.

infographic.key_insight: A finite element scheme for a heat-conduction hemivariational inequality converges strongly to the limit solution under both mesh refinement and increasing penalization, even when the two limits are taken independently or simultaneously.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a reliable numerical pathway for enforcing boundary temperature constraints in mixed-boundary thermal models while quantifying discretization accuracy.
method: Formulate the steady-state heat problem as a penalized hemivariational inequality with parameter α.
Discretize the penalized and limit problems using finite elements.
Prove double-limit convergence and derive an optimal-order error estimate for the discrete limit problem.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical convergence analysis supported by numerical simulations on four manufactured-solution examples.
infographic.watch_item: An error bound uniform in the penalization parameter α is not expected, so penalty selection must be handled carefully in implementation.
infographic.paper_title: Finite Element Approximation of a Hemivariational Inequality for Steady-State Heat Conduction: Double-Limit Convergence of Penalization and Discretization

title: Application and Evaluation of the Material Point Method for Low-Velocity Asteroid Collisions Involving Large Deformations
authors: Haru Fukuta, Tomoaki Ishiyama, Shu-ichiro Inutsuka
abstract: The collisional lifetimes of asteroids larger than $\sim 10$ km in the present-day main belt are estimated to exceed the age of the solar system, suggesting that their shapes may preserve memories of the collisional environment in the primordial solar system. Recent studies performed systematic simulations of equal-mass and low-velocity ($50$--$400\,\mathrm{ms}^{-1}$) collisions between 50-km-radius asteroids using Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH), identifying the impact conditions that produce irregular shapes. As an alternative approach, we here employ the Material Point Method (MPM), a particle-grid method well suited to large deformation of solids and free from tensile instability, and we assess its applicability to such systems by direct comparison with the established SPH results. We integrate a previously established rock model combined with a fracture model, the Tillotson equation of state, and Drucker-Prager friction, with the efficient non-associative Drucker-Prager plasticity solver originally developed for granular flows. We perform 135 collision simulations of equal-mass rocky asteroids spanning 15 impact velocities ($50$--$400\,\mathrm{ms}^{-1}$) and 9 impact angles ($5$--$45^\circ$), following the setup of the previous SPH simulations. The mass, axis ratio, and shape classification of the largest remnants closely reproduce the trends of the previous SPH simulations. Since most material transitions into a granular state early in the collision, this agreement appears to depend primarily on the validity of the frictional treatment of the granular material, rather than on the details of the fracture model. These results demonstrate the applicability of MPM to low-velocity asteroid collision simulations and support cross-validation between MPM- and SPH-based approaches.

infographic.key_insight: Material Point Method (MPM) can reproduce the main outcomes of low-velocity asteroid collision simulations with large deformations, matching prior SPH trends for remnant mass, shape, and classification.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This supports MPM as a practical, mesh-free tool for solid-body impact and fragmentation problems where large deformation and granular flow are critical.
method: 135 equal-mass rocky asteroid collisions were simulated across 15 impact speeds (50–400 m/s) and 9 impact angles (5–45°).
MPM coupled a rock/fracture model, Tillotson EOS, and Drucker–Prager friction with a non-associative plasticity solver.
Results were directly compared against established SPH collision studies under the same setup.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports close agreement with SPH in largest-remnant mass, axis ratio, and shape class across the parameter sweep.
infographic.watch_item: The agreement appears to depend mainly on the frictional granular treatment, so performance may be sensitive to constitutive assumptions rather than fracture details alone.
infographic.paper_title: Application and Evaluation of the Material Point Method for Low-Velocity Asteroid Collisions Involving Large Deformations

title: A hydrogen-informed Rice-Beltz model for crack-tip dislocation emission under mixed-mode loading
authors: Kai Zhao
abstract: The fundamental competition between crack-tip cleavage and dislocation emission dictates the ductile-to-brittle transition in crystalline solids. In hydrogen-charged environments, this delicate balance is disrupted, yet existing models often struggle to self-consistently capture the atomic-scale thermomechanical modulation of the emission barrier. Here, we propose the hydrogen-informed Rice-Beltz framework to quantify the critical stress intensity factors (SIFs) required for initial dislocation nucleation under mixed-mode (I+II) loading. By integrating the elastic interaction of the dilatational field of interstitial hydrogen and the applied stress fields against the incipient dislocation core, the model recovers the non-monotonic relation between the most probable SIF and the hydrogen concentration. Unlike the classical pure mode-I (or mode-II) scenario, the minimization of the local strain energy density is employed to generate closed-form nominal driving forces, which are subsequently embedded into a transition-state-theory framework. This atomistically-informed approach yields the most probable SIF for the first dislocation emission event as a function of the loading rate, slip angle, and hydrogen concentration, providing a rigorous, parameter-free boundary condition for the onset of hydrogen-modulated crack-tip plasticity.

infographic.key_insight: A hydrogen-informed Rice-Beltz model predicts crack-tip dislocation emission under mixed-mode loading by coupling hydrogen-induced stress-field interactions with a transition-state barrier for nucleation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It provides a parameter-free way to estimate when hydrogen will shift the crack-tip response from cleavage toward plasticity, helping assess hydrogen embrittlement risk in crystalline solids.
method: Extends the Rice-Beltz framework to mixed-mode I+II crack-tip loading.
Includes elastic interaction between interstitial hydrogen dilatation fields and the incipient dislocation core.
Uses local strain energy density minimization plus transition-state theory to derive critical stress intensity factors.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports closed-form predictions that reproduce a non-monotonic relationship between the most probable stress intensity factor and hydrogen concentration, along with dependence on loading rate, slip angle, and hydrogen content.
infographic.watch_item: The model is atomistically informed but still analytical, so its accuracy depends on how well the assumed core energetics and hydrogen-field interactions represent the specific material and loading path.
infographic.paper_title: A hydrogen-informed Rice-Beltz model for crack-tip dislocation emission under mixed-mode loading

title: Experimental and numerical study of shock wave propagation in water generated by pulsed arc electrohydraulic discharges
authors: Wen Chen, Olivier Maurel, Christian La Borderie, Thierry Reess, Antoine Silvestre de Ferron, Mohammed Matallah
abstract: The objective of this study is to simulate the propagation of the shock wave in water due to an explosion. The study is part of a global research program on the development of an alternative stimulation technique to conventional hydraulic fracturing in tight gas reservoirs aimed at inducing a distributed state of microcracking of rocks instead of localized fracture. We consider the possibility of increasing the permeability of rocks with dynamic blasts. The blast is a shock wave generated in water by pulsed arc electrohydraulic discharges. The amplitude of these shock waves is prescribed by the electrohydraulic discharges which generate high pressures of several kilobars within microseconds. A simplified method has been used to simulate the injected electrical energy as augmentation of enthalpy in water locally. The finite element code EUROPLEXUS is used to perform fluid fast dynamic computation. The predicted pressure is consistent with the experimental results. In addition, shock wave propagation characteristics predicted with simulation can be valuable reference for design of underwater structural elements and engineering of underwater explosion.

infographic.key_insight: Pulsed arc electrohydraulic discharges in water generate microsecond-scale kilobar shock waves that can be modeled numerically by locally adding electrical energy as enthalpy.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The results help assess dynamic blast-based stimulation for increasing rock permeability and provide guidance for underwater explosion and structural design.
method: Simulated shock propagation in water with the EUROPLEXUS finite element code.
Represented injected electrical energy as a localized enthalpy increase in the fluid.
Compared predicted pressure evolution against experiments.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that the predicted pressure is consistent with the experimental results.
infographic.watch_item: The enthalpy-injection model is a simplified representation of the discharge physics, so transferability to other geometries or materials should be checked carefully.
infographic.paper_title: Experimental and numerical study of shock wave propagation in water generated by pulsed arc electrohydraulic discharges

title: Hydrogen-stabilized multimodal high-index twin network in iron
authors: Mehrab Lotfpour, Haoran Cui, Yan Wang, Eduardo Vitral, Lei Cao
abstract: Hydrogen significantly affects plasticity in bcc iron, but its role is commonly attributed to dislocation-mediated mechanisms, leaving the influence of hydrogen on phase transformation and deformation twinning poorly understood. We use a density-functional-theory-trained deep-neural-network interatomic potential and large-scale molecular dynamics to study pure bcc Fe and Fe containing 10% hydrogen. It is found that hydrogen lowers the yield stress but, more importantly, increases the persistence of {112} twin variants and suppresses detwinning. This effect stabilizes an interconnected {332}-{10 9 3} multimodal twin network and produces pronounced post-yield hardening. Higher temperature promotes the initial transformation but weakens the persistence of the high-index multimodal twin network. Moreover, twinning follows distinct loading-dependent pathways: compression generates {332} and {10 9 3} boundaries through co-zone and non-co-zone twin-twin interactions, whereas tension produces {7 4 1} boundaries through non-co-zone interactions. These results establish a pathway-based picture in which the intermediate phase determines the accessible twin modes and variant crystallography, while hydrogen and temperature control their kinetic survival and the emergence of high-index twin networks.

infographic.key_insight: Hydrogen in bcc iron not only lowers yield stress, but also stabilizes a multimodal high-index twin network by prolonging {112} twin variants and suppressing detwinning.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This suggests hydrogen can strongly alter hardening, twinning pathways, and failure-relevant deformation behavior in iron-based structural materials.
method: DFT-trained deep-neural-network interatomic potential
Large-scale molecular dynamics simulations
Comparison of pure bcc Fe versus Fe with 10% hydrogen across loading, temperature, and tension/compression
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports simulation evidence that hydrogen and temperature change twin variant persistence, detwinning, and the emergence of {332}-{10 9 3} and {7 4 1} twin boundaries under different loading paths.
infographic.watch_item: Results are based on atomistic simulation with a specific hydrogen concentration, so transferability to real microstructures, defect populations, and lower H levels may require experimental validation.
infographic.paper_title: Hydrogen-stabilized multimodal high-index twin network in iron

title: Beyond Compression: Training Latent Representations for Stable Long-Horizon Rollout in Neural Surrogate Solvers
authors: Andreas E. Robertson, Ashley T. Lenau, John D. Shimanek, Benjamin A. Jasperson, Vivek Oommen, David L. Damm
abstract: Latent neural surrogate solvers, or latent dynamics models, accelerate simulations of time-dependent physical systems by evolving a compressed latent space rather than resolving full-resolution fields directly. In principle this reduces computational cost and simplifies learning, but in practice errors often accumulate rapidly during long autoregressive rollouts, limiting predictive utility. We show that this instability does not stem from the latent representation itself, but arises when it is trained solely for reconstruction, producing representations poorly suited to long-horizon forecasting. We systematically evaluate training-level interventions that align latent representations with long-horizon rollout: Koopman operator learning and Hamming noise injection during autoencoder training to improve compression, together with noise injection and multi-step rollout fine-tuning to improve dynamics. Interventions that improve long-horizon rollout stability often degrade conventional training metrics, including reconstruction and one-step prediction accuracy. Collectively, these interventions reduce long-rollout error by approximately 40\% and match or exceed the accuracy of full-resolution models on two physics benchmarks, while requiring 2 orders of magnitude fewer floating point operations and half the GPU memory. Applied to mesoscale crystal-plasticity simulations of high-cycle fatigue, the resulting surrogate achieves stable extrapolation over horizons orders of magnitude beyond those observed during training. More broadly, these results show that neural compression should be designed not merely to reduce dimensionality, but to restructure the solution space for stable dynamical evolution, a key requirement for reliable, efficient neural surrogates in scientific applications.

infographic.key_insight: Latent surrogate solvers fail in long rollouts mainly because their representations are trained for reconstruction, not stable dynamics, so the latent space must be shaped for forecasting rather than compression alone.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For solid mechanics surrogates, training the latent space for rollout stability can cut compute and memory dramatically while preserving or improving long-horizon prediction on expensive time-dependent simulations.
method: Train latent spaces with Koopman operator learning to better support linearizable long-term dynamics.
Add Hamming noise during autoencoder training and noise injection during dynamics training to improve robustness.
Fine-tune with multi-step rollout objectives to reduce error accumulation over long horizons.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across two physics benchmarks and mesoscale crystal-plasticity fatigue simulations, these interventions reduced long-rollout error by about 40%, matched or exceeded full-resolution accuracy, and used roughly 100x fewer FLOPs and half the GPU memory.
infographic.watch_item: Methods that improve rollout stability can hurt reconstruction and one-step accuracy, so implementation must balance standard training metrics against long-horizon performance.
infographic.paper_title: Beyond Compression: Training Latent Representations for Stable Long-Horizon Rollout in Neural Surrogate Solvers

title: Optimal Recovery for Solving Variational Problems
authors: Ting Wang, Gideon Simpson, Jaroslaw Knap
abstract: In science and engineering, many physical laws and scientific principles naturally arise as variational problems of minimizing an energy functional over an appropriate functional space. In many cases, it is more advantageous to directly discover the minimizer of the energy functional than to solve the associated Euler-Lagrange equations. Conventional numerical solvers, such as the finite-element method (FEM), often lack the flexibility to incorporate prior knowledge or noisy observational data. In recent years, machine learning approaches, particularly kernel-based methods, have attracted growing attention in scientific computing. Unlike FEM, which requires domain discretization and mesh generation, kernel-based methods construct solutions from scattered nodes, thereby avoiding the complexity of meshing, especially in high-dimensional or geometrically complex domains. This works presents a two-step procedure for variational energy minimization based on the optimal recovery formulation in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS), providing a unified framework for seamlessly incorporating both physical constraints and noisy data. On the computational side, we employ the sparse Cholesky decomposition for Matérn kernels to alleviate the well-known cubic complexity bottleneck of kernel methods. On the theoretical side, we rigorously establish the existence and convergence theory of the proposed method using $Γ$-convergence theory. Numerical experiments on benchmark problems demonstrate the efficiency, robustness and accuracy of the approach.

infographic.key_insight: The paper reframes variational PDE solving as an optimal recovery problem in an RKHS, enabling direct minimization of energy with both physics and noisy data enforced in one framework.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This offers a mesh-free surrogate strategy for solid mechanics and other engineering PDEs, especially useful when domains are complex or observational data must be assimilated.
method: Two-step variational minimization via optimal recovery in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space.
Use Matérn kernels with sparse Cholesky decomposition to reduce kernel-method computational cost.
Prove existence and convergence with Γ-convergence theory.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports numerical experiments on benchmark problems showing efficiency, robustness, and accuracy.
infographic.watch_item: Kernel methods can still be computationally demanding at scale, so sparse factorization and kernel choice are critical for practical performance.
infographic.paper_title: Optimal Recovery for Solving Variational Problems

title: High-order energy diminishing ALE-SAV finite element methods for two-phase Navier--Stokes flow
authors: Shu Ma
abstract: We develop a high-order fully discrete ALE-SAV finite element method for sharp-interface two-phase Navier--Stokes flow that satisfies a discrete energy dissipation law. We introduce an SAV reformulation to ensure the stable treatment of the surface and gravitational potential energies, together with an energy-stable ALE transfer operator that controls the density-weighted kinetic energy across moving meshes. The resulting scheme is linear and satisfies a modified energy-dissipation inequality. Numerical experiments, including rising-bubble benchmarks, demonstrate the robustness of the method and confirm second-order convergence in time and arbitrarily high-order convergence in space.

infographic.key_insight: The paper proposes a high-order ALE-SAV finite element scheme that preserves a discrete energy-dissipation law for sharp-interface two-phase Navier--Stokes flow on moving meshes.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a stable, linear, and high-accuracy tool for simulating multiphase flows with evolving interfaces, such as bubbles, droplets, and free-surface dynamics.
method: Uses a scalar auxiliary variable (SAV) reformulation to handle surface and gravitational potential energies stably.
Introduces an energy-stable ALE transfer operator to control density-weighted kinetic energy across mesh motion.
Builds a fully discrete finite element method with modified energy-dissipation inequality and high-order accuracy in time and space.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports rising-bubble benchmark tests and shows second-order convergence in time with arbitrarily high-order convergence in space.
infographic.watch_item: The method is linear and stable, but practical performance may depend on careful implementation of the ALE transfer operator and moving-mesh handling.
infographic.paper_title: High-order energy diminishing ALE-SAV finite element methods for two-phase Navier--Stokes flow

title: Event-by-event track imaging of charged particles with an ultrafast plenoptic camera
authors: Till Dieminger, Marco Barbieri, Vincenzo Berardi, Saúl Alonso-Monsalve, Kodai Kaneyasu, Paul Mos
abstract: Modern elementary particle detectors often require high-resolution three-dimensional particle tracking in large dense active volumes, which is difficult to achieve in standard devices without an extremely fine segmentation. In recent work, a plenoptic camera instrumented with a single-photon avalanche-diode array, called PLATON, demonstrated to image individual visible photons generated in monolithic scintillating material and reconstruct their three-dimensional origin from a single-event exposure, opening a route to high-spatial-resolution detection of elementary particles in unsegmented scintillator. However, those tests aimed to address photon sources of essentially zero geometric extent. In this work we close the gap to the tracking regime. First, we calibrated the PLATON prototype using light tracks in an organic plastic scintillator induced by a femtosecond infrared laser via two-photon absorption and characterised its capability to reconstruct photon-starved 3D lines with a novel algorithm, achieving good agreement with custom Monte Carlo simulation. Finally, the PLATON prototype was exposed to a test beam of pions at the CERN Proton Synchrotron. For the first time, a plenoptic detector system was successfully used to detect and reconstruct the 3D tracks of elementary particles from 2D photon-starved images on an event-by-event basis marking a transformative approach to high-resolution measurements.

infographic.key_insight: An ultrafast plenoptic camera can reconstruct individual charged-particle tracks in 3D from photon-starved, single-event scintillator images.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables high-resolution particle tracking in unsegmented detector volumes, reducing the need for extremely fine physical segmentation.
method: Calibrated the PLATON plenoptic SPAD-array prototype with laser-induced scintillation tracks in plastic scintillator.
Used a novel reconstruction algorithm to recover 3D photon-starved line trajectories.
Validated performance against custom Monte Carlo simulation and then test-beam pion data at CERN.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports good agreement with custom Monte Carlo simulations and successful event-by-event reconstruction of 3D pion tracks from 2D photon-starved images.
infographic.watch_item: Performance was demonstrated on a prototype and controlled test-beam setup, so robustness in larger-scale detector systems and higher-background conditions still needs verification.
infographic.paper_title: Event-by-event track imaging of charged particles with an ultrafast plenoptic camera

title: Environmental requirements for the use of social information by artificial life agents using evolved plastic artificial neural networks
authors: Hugh Charterton, James M. Borg, Aniko Ekart
abstract: Evolved Plastic Artificial Neural Networks (EPANNs) consist of two principal processes, the first, evolution, and the second, development and in-life learning. In the context of the origins of social = learning, very few studies have been carried out using ALIFE models based on EPANN requirements. Studies in this field have usually involved an imitative teacher/pupil relationship. This, however, ignores the possibility that the observed behaviour is a consequence of social information cues rather than direct imitation or teaching. Starting with the first of the EPANN processes (evolution), a series of experiments was undertaken using artificial neural network (ANN) based agents in a variety of foraging environments to examine under what minimal environmental conditions the use of social information might have evolved, as measured by the number of generations taken to meet a specified fitness criterion. NEAT (Neuroevolution of Augmenting Topologies) was the ANN used as its evolutionary algorithm would evolve a network's topology as well its weights. Unintentionally, in the experiment there was a simple network topology based on the location of the nearest food item which enabled agents to swiftly meet the fitness criterion. With this topology, additional information, social or otherwise, was not required and could have proved to be a hindrance. However, this does indicate that for the use of social information to have evolved, it would require a greater degree of complexity in the environment to do so.

infographic.key_insight: In simple foraging environments, evolved ANN agents can solve the task using direct environmental cues alone, so social information is unlikely to evolve unless the environment is more complex.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For artificial life and adaptive robotics, this suggests that richer task structure may be necessary before social learning mechanisms provide a measurable benefit.
method: Used NEAT to evolve both network topology and weights in EPANN-based agents.
Tested agents in multiple foraging environments to assess when social information might be favored.
Measured performance by generations required to reach a predefined fitness criterion.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across the experiments, a simple topology based on the nearest food location let agents meet the fitness criterion quickly, reducing any need for social or extra information.
infographic.watch_item: The observed advantage may depend strongly on environment simplicity, so results should not be generalized to settings where social cues could matter more.
infographic.paper_title: Environmental requirements for the use of social information by artificial life agents using evolved plastic artificial neural networks

title: Learn Here, Move Less Elsewhere: Input-Conditioned Plasticity from Retained-Domain Activation Atlases
authors: Jiangtao Lin, Bangyang Wei, Yihang Ding, Siyi Liu, Yuhan Dong
abstract: Task-specific fine-tuning can rewrite a language model's answers beyond the training task, complicating updates that must preserve existing behavior. We introduce ATLAS, which turns retained-domain representations into an input-dependent rule for task adaptation. An activation atlas supplies local reference centers and directional filters to a shared low-rank residual. Target supervision learns the residual, while retained geometry shapes its action throughout training and inference. On Qwen3-8B, ATLAS achieves lower mean retained-output Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence than all seven published baselines at shared coding-performance requirements, with consistent advantages across multiple training seeds. Structural comparisons identify the contributions of retained reference states and directional conditioning, and answer-level analyses show fewer rewritten mathematical answers and more stable commonsense choices. Experiments spanning five backbones and two retained domains further demonstrate coding gains with reduced retained-output movement. With compact storage and modest decoding overhead, ATLAS provides a practical mechanism for acquiring specialized skills while maintaining continuity in existing responses.

infographic.key_insight: ATLAS makes fine-tuning input-conditioned by using retained-domain activation geometry to control a low-rank residual, helping a model learn new skills without rewriting unrelated behavior.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For constitutive-modeling-style workflows, this suggests a practical way to specialize a shared surrogate or operator while preserving previously validated responses and reducing regression risk.
method: Build an activation atlas from retained-domain representations to define local reference centers.
Use directional filters from the atlas to condition a shared low-rank residual during training and inference.
Train on task supervision while constraining updates through retained-domain geometry to limit off-task drift.
infographic.evidence_signal: On Qwen3-8B, ATLAS reports the lowest mean retained-output KL divergence among seven published baselines at matched coding performance, with consistent gains across multiple random seeds and broader tests on five backbones and two retained domains.
infographic.watch_item: The added atlas conditioning and decoding overhead are modest, but deployment still needs careful storage management and validation that the retained-domain atlas remains representative as tasks or domains change.
infographic.paper_title: Learn Here, Move Less Elsewhere: Input-Conditioned Plasticity from Retained-Domain Activation Atlases

title: A Comparative Study on Robust Topology Optimization of Design-Dependent Pressure-Actuated Compliant Mechanisms with Quadrilateral Elements
authors: Swagatam Islam Sarkar, Prabhat Kumar
abstract: This paper presents a comparative study of compliant mechanisms generated using a robust topology optimization technique involving design-dependent pressure loads. Design domains are parameterized using standard and higher-order quadrilateral elements. Both eroded and blueprint configurations are considered. A min-max optimization model combined with an output-spring method is employed to extremize the mechanisms' output displacements. A volume and a strain energy constraint are applied to the blueprint and the eroded designs, respectively. The optimization process is executed using the method of moving asymptotes. Numerical experiments are performed to optimize the pressure-actuated inverter and gripper mechanisms using Q4, Q8, and Q9 elements, and the results are compared. The research highlights how quadrilateral element selection influences both the resulting topologies and performance characteristics.

infographic.key_insight: Using robust topology optimization with design-dependent pressure loads, the paper shows that quadrilateral element order (Q4/Q8/Q9) materially changes both the final compliant mechanism topology and its actuation performance.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This is relevant for designing pressure-actuated compliant mechanisms because it helps engineers choose element formulations that better capture robust, manufacturable performance under uncertainty.
method: Min-max robust topology optimization with blueprint and eroded configurations
Design-dependent pressure load handling via an output-spring method
MMA-based optimization for inverter and gripper benchmarks using Q4, Q8, and Q9 elements
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports numerical experiments on pressure-actuated inverter and gripper mechanisms, comparing optimized topologies and performance across Q4, Q8, and Q9 discretizations.
infographic.watch_item: Results may be sensitive to mesh/element choice and the specific robust formulation, so cross-comparison across discretizations should be interpreted carefully.
infographic.paper_title: A Comparative Study on Robust Topology Optimization of Design-Dependent Pressure-Actuated Compliant Mechanisms with Quadrilateral Elements

title: KATOsuper: Surrogate-accelerated neural topology optimization with sensitivity-consistent Fourier neural operators
authors: Shengyu Yan, Jasmin Jelovica
abstract: Topology optimization (TO) remains computationally intensive due to repeated finite element analysis (FEA) evaluations required at each iteration. While neural network-based surrogates offer potential acceleration, existing approaches often suffer from gradient inconsistency between predicted objectives and sensitivities, leading to optimization instability. This work presents KATOsuper, an objective-agnostic framework that couples neural-reparameterized topology optimization with a Sensitivity-Consistent Fourier Neural Operator (SC-FNO). The framework employs the forward_split architecture, which derives deployed sensitivities via automatic differentiation through the predicted objective field and thereby preserves consistency between the predicted objective and the gradient used for optimization. The case studies include three 2D benchmark problems and three 3D structures considering compliance or stress minimization. A physics-informed multi-channel input encoding with Fourier position embedding enables resolution-invariant learning, supporting zero-shot extrapolation beyond the training resolution, with useful performance at moderate scaling factors and topology-preserving exploration at up to 64x without retraining. The framework extends to 3D through KATO3D, featuring novel KANConv3D blocks with learnable B-spline activations. KATOsuper demonstrates 15--110x deployment-time speedup over MATLAB baselines while maintaining competitive optimality, with the clearest gains observed in complex 3D and stress-optimization cases. The insight that sensitivity direction matters more than magnitude enables robust optimization even with approximate physics evaluation, extensible to other differentiable physics-driven design objectives.

infographic.key_insight: KATOsuper makes topology optimization faster and more stable by using a sensitivity-consistent Fourier neural operator so the predicted objective and its gradient stay aligned during optimization.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables practical surrogate-accelerated compliance and stress design for 2D and 3D structures, with large deployment-time speedups while preserving competitive topology quality.
method: Forward_split SC-FNO computes sensitivities by automatic differentiation through the predicted objective field.
Physics-informed multi-channel inputs plus Fourier position embeddings support resolution-invariant learning and zero-shot extrapolation.
KATO3D extends the framework to 3D with KANConv3D blocks and learnable B-spline activations.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across three 2D benchmarks and three 3D cases, the method reports about 15–110x deployment-time speedup over MATLAB baselines, with stronger gains in complex 3D and stress-optimization problems.
infographic.watch_item: Zero-shot scaling can preserve topology at high resolution factors, but practical accuracy depends on consistent sensitivity direction, so approximation error in the physics surrogate still needs careful validation.
infographic.paper_title: KATOsuper: Surrogate-accelerated neural topology optimization with sensitivity-consistent Fourier neural operators

title: EngramRAG: Dynamic Usage-Weighted Topology and Synaptic Consolidation for Multi-Hop Agentic Memory
authors: Bhavyateja Potineni, Lohit Giri, Anu Jain, Vadim Kutsyy, Rajasekhar Pentakota
abstract: As autonomous LLM agents are deployed across multi-session environments, conventional memory architectures suffer from Associative Blindness (inability to traverse multi-hop relational dependencies), Scaffolding Amnesia (temporal decay evicting core persona invariants), and Static Topology Stagnation (immutable graphs ignoring usage dynamics). Grounded in Complementary Learning Systems (CLS) principles, we propose EngramRAG, an adaptive memory architecture coupling a low-latency Waking State reflex with an asynchronous background Dreaming State consolidation cycle. EngramRAG introduces: (1) Usage-Modulated Personalized PageRank (U-PPR), where transition probabilities adapt via Hebbian plasticity to promote persistent entities into high-centrality Epistemic Macro-Hubs; (2) Consolidation-Activated Topology Decay (CATD), which scales retention half-life by topological load-bearing weight rather than wall-clock recency, protected by a cold-start grace period (N_grace >= 4); (3) Directed SUPERSEDES DAG filtering to suppress obsolete state during fact mutations; and (4) Triple-source hybrid retrieval fusing dense vectors, BM25, and U-PPR via dynamic Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF). Evaluating on all 1,982 QA pairs across 10 long-term conversations in the LoCoMo benchmark, EngramRAG achieves +38.9% relative improvement in Recall@5 (53.21% vs. 38.29%, p < 0.001) and +43.1% in MRR (0.4203 vs. 0.2937) over dense vector RAG, significantly outperforming Okapi BM25 (48.66%) and isolated static graph retrieval (8.50%). On temporal reasoning, EngramRAG reaches 62.33% Recall@5 (+16.67 points over dense vectors). In controlled mutation tests, SUPERSEDES suppresses split-brain hallucinations from 70.0% to 0.0%, while 90-day simulations show 100.0% scaffolding retention under a 26.21ms interactive retrieval reflex.

infographic.key_insight: EngramRAG turns agent memory into an adaptive, usage-weighted graph that learns which facts to keep, which links to strengthen, and which obsolete states to suppress across long conversations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For autonomous engineering agents, this architecture improves multi-hop retrieval and long-term state consistency, which are critical for reliable decision support, design workflows, and persistent personas.
method: Usage-Modulated Personalized PageRank (U-PPR) boosts frequently useful entities into stable high-centrality hubs.
Consolidation-Activated Topology Decay (CATD) preserves load-bearing memories based on graph importance rather than simple recency.
SUPERSEDES and hybrid RRF retrieval combine dense vectors, BM25, and graph signals to reduce stale or conflicting memory.
infographic.evidence_signal: On LoCoMo’s 1,982 QA pairs, EngramRAG improved Recall@5 to 53.21% versus 38.29% for dense RAG and raised MRR to 0.4203, while eliminating split-brain hallucinations in mutation tests.
infographic.watch_item: The system adds algorithmic and operational complexity, so real-world deployment must manage tuning, latency stability, and robustness of graph maintenance at scale.
infographic.paper_title: EngramRAG: Dynamic Usage-Weighted Topology and Synaptic Consolidation for Multi-Hop Agentic Memory
